title: A Interior for the Glasshouse
premise: Mara Nakamura has spent fifteen years writing letters to his sister Yuki at an address that no longer exists, maintaining the fiction that she simply moved away rather than the truth the whole Nakamura family agreed to bury: that Yuki died in the fire that destroyed the glasshouse their father built, a fire Mara set accidentally and everyone silently blamed him for. When the family home goes up for auction, Mara returns to the old neighborhood and finds his mother, his uncle, and his estranged father each carrying their own version of the night, each having arranged their silence around protecting someone else. As the auction deadline forces every secret into the open, Mara learns Yuki's death was neither his fault nor an accident, and that his mother's letters to him were as fabricated as his were to her. The novel ends with Mara delivering one last letter, this time to a real address, choosing truth over the loyalty that kept his family intact and broken at once.
about_author: Paloma Amberdale is the pen name of a former estate auctioneer who spent a decade cataloguing the contents of other people's lives before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted conservatory in coastal Oregon, where she keeps an unsent letter of her own in a drawer she opens exactly once a year.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. We meet Mara in his meticulous routine: composing postcards to Yuki at the burned address, cataloguing what he cannot say, and working as an archivist who organizes other people's memories for a living. A letter arrives announcing the auction of the Nakamura house. Emotional beat: the fragile equilibrium of a life built on avoidance, about to crack.

chapters.title: Postcards to a Burned Address
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Flashbacks interleave with his journey back to the old neighborhood: the glasshouse his father built, the closeness with Yuki, the night of the fire he remembers in fragments. He checks into a motel near the ruins. Emotional beat: grief resurfacing as physical dread; the past has a geography and he has just re-entered it.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara walks the empty house before the auction, finding Yuki's room untouched, a child's drawing hidden in a wall cavity that suggests she saw something the night of the fire. Emotional beat: the first fissure in his guilt—evidence that the story he was handed may not be the story that happened.

chapters.title: The Mother Who Filed Everything
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: his mother, Emiko. She is cataloguing her own belongings for the auction with the same precision Mara inherited. We learn she has kept every one of Mara's postcards, and that she has written letters of her own she never sent. Emotional beat: the revelation that silence in this family was a shared craft, practiced from both directions.

chapters.title: Uncle Ren's Version
chapters.summary: Uncle Ren's POV. At a neighborhood bar, Ren, who was first on the scene the night of the fire, tells Mara a version of events with a detail that doesn't fit: the glasshouse doors were locked from the outside. Emotional beat: loyalty curdling into complicity; Ren has carried the detail for fifteen years and is deciding, drink by drink, whether to give it away.

chapters.title: The Father at the Auction Preview
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. At the preview event, Mara confronts his father, Kenji, who has not spoken to him since the funeral. Kenji deflects with talk of lot numbers and valuations, but Mara notices the auction catalog lists the glasshouse foundation as 'unimproved land'—his father is trying to erase it from the record entirely. Emotional beat: love expressed as erasure, duty as denial.

chapters.title: The Locked Door
chapters.summary: Emiko's POV. Emiko, pressed by the approaching auction and Mara's questions, finally opens her locked cedar chest: inside are the insurance investigator's original report and Yuki's diary. She confesses she has known the truth for years and chose the family's survival over Mara's. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of protection—what she traded, and for whom.

chapters.title: Everything the Family Arranged Itself Around
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara reads the report and diary together: the fire was arson, set by Kenji for the insurance money, with Yuki inside; the locked door was his doing. The family's silence protected the arsonist, not the child. Emotional beat: the climax—guilt inverted into fury, loyalty revealed as the mechanism of the crime itself.

chapters.title: The Last Lot
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with Kenji's interludes. At the auction, as the house lot comes up, Mara stands and reads Yuki's diary aloud before the assembled neighborhood. Kenji does not deny it. The sale collapses; the family fractures in public what had only fractured in private. Emotional beat: truth spoken at maximum cost—no rescue, no softening, only the act itself.

chapters.title: A Letter to a Real Address
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Months later, Mara visits Yuki's grave for the first time, then writes one final postcard—not to the burned address, but to Emiko, who has moved to a small apartment and asked, for the first time, to hear from him. He mails it. Emotional beat: resolution without repair; love relearned on honest terms, and the inventory of unsaid things finally, partially, spoken.
